issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of natural disaster. Generic sensory cues can fit disaster trauma, but snakes and babies are highly specific cues with no clear link to a natural disaster and, taken together with body odour, suggest unrelated trigger themes rather than a single trauma network.

Within the overall profile, the memory/appraisal content is also mismatched. 'Intense shame on recall' usually implies a strong negative appraisal/self-evaluative theme, yet no Negative Appraisals items are endorsed and that node is formulation-wise disconnected. For a natural disaster survivor, shame can occur, but as the only explicit meaning-based memory item it sits awkwardly with otherwise cue-driven fragmented recall and no corresponding appraisal content.

'Babies' as an auditory trigger is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma in this profile unless there is specific undisclosed trauma content involving infants; the other triggers (loud noises, sweat/body odour) are more disaster-congruent, so this item stands out as clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers mainly with memory and only minimally with maladaptive strategies, and the other selected items suggest intrusive sensory recall rather than an anger/interpersonal-dysregulation pattern. This coping item appears to target a symptom style not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' is likewise poorly supported by the rest of the profile. With no threat or negative appraisal content selected and memory items focused on fragmentation/triggered recall, this strategy lacks a clear cognitive-affective anchor in the chosen profile and is difficult to connect specifically to natural-disaster PTSD here.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, sweat/body odour and alcohol smell are hard to link plausibly as primary trauma reminders unless there is additional disaster-specific context (e.g., shelter crowding, intoxicated bystanders). Loud noises fit, but these two olfactory triggers are clinically difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but as the only affective memory item here it is a poor fit with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes sensory triggering and fragmented involuntary recall rather than self-blame, humiliation, or morally charged memory content. This makes the memory node less coherent with the trauma type and the selected triggers/strategies.

Alcohol smell is a hard-to-explain trigger for a natural-disaster trauma in the absence of any matching trauma context or linked appraisal content; loud noise and smoke are coherent disaster-related cues, but alcohol odor stands out as clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but with no negative-appraisal content and no other memory material suggesting shame-linked actions or moral failure, this item is poorly supported and clinically discordant with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Alcohol Use: drink alcohol
issues.explanation: Using alcohol can occur nonspecifically, but paired with an alcohol-smell trigger it implies trauma meaning centered on alcohol-related cues that is not represented elsewhere in the disaster-based trigger or memory profile, reducing coherence.

vignette:
# Carlos

Carlos was thirty-eight when Hurricane María made landfall on Puerto Rico in September 2017. He had been working a double shift at San Juan Hospital, exhausted but necessary—the storm surge warnings had sent half his colleagues home early to secure their families, and the emergency department was understaffed. He was in the surgical wing when the windows began to shatter. The sound came first, a deafening shriek of wind that seemed to peel the roof open, followed by the percussion of glass and metal, the roar of water breaching the lower floors. Then came the smell—acrid, chemical, the burning of electrical systems and the thick, choking reek of smoke as a fire started in the east corridor. Carlos had tried to move toward it, muscle memory from training overriding the chaos, but the attending had grabbed him, pulled him back into a stairwell. He remembered fragments with crystalline clarity: the face of a nursing assistant trapped behind a collapsed beam on the third floor, the heat of the fire at his back as they evacuated, the taste of ash and salt water mixed in his mouth. But there were gaps—long stretches of the evacuation itself were missing, as though his mind had simply stopped recording. He could not account for nearly forty minutes. He knew he had made it to the parking garage, knew he had driven home in standing water, but the middle was blank. What he could not forget was the smell, and the sound, and the overwhelming sense that he had abandoned people who needed him.

The years that followed were a slow settling into a life that looked normal from the outside. Carlos had returned to work within weeks. He and his wife María had rebuilt their home. They had settled into a comfortable routine in San Juan, and to most observers—his colleagues, his extended family—he seemed fine. But fine was a careful construction. When a car backfired near the hospital, or when he heard the sharp crack of fireworks during a neighborhood celebration, Carlos's body would jolt as though electrified. The sound would pull him back to that stairwell instantly, completely, and he would feel the heat and smell the smoke with an immediacy that made his hands shake. His mind would fragment again—the same gaps, the same missing time, the same crushing guilt about the people he could not reach. To manage these moments, he had developed a pattern. When the intrusions came, when the memories surfaced unbidden and the grief felt like it might split him open, he would leave work early, claiming fatigue or a patient complication that required follow-up. He would go home and lose himself in sexual fantasies, or he would drink—carefully at first, a glass of wine in the evening, then two, then a glass before work. The alcohol seemed to blur the edges of the memories, to create distance between himself and the gaps he could not fill. He took sleeping pills when the nightmares came, and occasionally he would use stronger things when the combination of triggers and memories became too much to bear.

María had begun to notice the pattern months ago. She would find him in his study late at night, a drink in hand, or she would realize he had left work without explanation. When she asked him about it, he could not articulate what was happening—could not explain that certain sounds seemed to crack open the sealed-off parts of that day, or that when the memories surfaced, he needed to do something, anything, to make them stop. What frightened him most was the incompleteness of it all, the knowledge that something crucial had happened in those lost minutes, something that might have changed the outcome if he could only remember it. The more he drank to escape the memories, the more fragmented they became, the more he needed to escape. His colleagues had begun to comment on his absences, on the slight tremor in his hands during complex procedures. His relationship with María had grown distant and strained. He had come to believe that the gaps in his memory were his fault, that his mind was punishing him for his failure, and that no amount of distraction or chemical relief could fill the space where his certainty used to be.

It was María who finally insisted he seek help, after finding him passed out in his study at three in the afternoon, an empty bottle beside him and the smell of smoke—from a neighbor's barbecue—having triggered a cascade he could no longer manage alone. Carlos sat in the therapist's office now, forty years old and terrified that looking directly at what he had forgotten would only make it worse.
